payload.throughline: Use experimental conditions to predict protein movement, then use interface complementarity and conformational cycling to infer bounded nonenzymatic function.

curriculum_context.canonical_title: Analyze protein separation and nonenzymatic function

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: compare pH with pI. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: decide what property the method makes decisive—native charge, isoelectric point, or size—before predicting movement.
No prerequisite lesson is declared. Use the supplied pH, pI, electrode labels, and treatment conditions rather than assuming a memorized apparatus.

The isoelectric point, pI, is the pH at which a protein has approximately zero net charge. At pH below its pI, the protein is more protonated and net positive; at pH above its pI, it is more deprotonated and net negative.

In an electric field, a net-positive protein migrates toward the negative electrode, while a net-negative protein migrates toward the positive electrode. Near its pI, charge-driven migration is minimal.
Isoelectric focusing uses a pH gradient. Each protein moves until local pH equals its pI, where its net charge approaches zero and focusing occurs.
SDS treatment denatures proteins and supplies a broadly similar negative charge-to-mass ratio. In SDS-PAGE, smaller polypeptides generally move farther through the gel than larger ones.
Native electrophoresis can reflect charge, size, and shape together. Do not use an SDS size-only rule unless the treatment is stated.
Mental model: method conditions → decisive property → protein state → charge sign or effective size → direction and relative migration.

Think aloud: protein P has pI 5.5 and the buffer is pH 8.0, so pH is above pI and P is net negative. With electrodes labelled, I send it toward the positive electrode. I do not apply a size-only rule because SDS was not stated.

Worked example: proteins A and B have pI values 4.8 and 8.2 in an isoelectric-focusing gradient spanning pH 3–10. A focuses at the more acidic position near pH 4.8; B focuses at the more basic position near pH 8.2.
Selection reasoning: focusing position follows pI, not molecular mass, because local pH determines when net charge reaches approximately zero.
Guided practice: use the visible condition-to-behavior frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh protein case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: “negative protein” is not a permanent identity; net charge depends on pH. SDS-PAGE size ranking does not transfer automatically to native electrophoresis or isoelectric focusing.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required inference changes.
Near-function repair: Anchor the sign: below pI is positive, at pI is near neutral, and above pI is negative. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.

Changed-function repair: In an increasing left-to-right pH gradient, each protein focuses where the pH reaches its pI. Compare pI values to order positions: lower pI sits left of higher pI. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: compare two new pI values to place both proteins in a different increasing-pH gradient, rechecking the failed exit’s exact KC, function, and operation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: identify the method, compare pH with pI, assign charge sign, follow the electrode labels, and reserve size-only ranking for stated SDS conditions.
Starting check: infer binding from complementarity. This low-stakes check does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: infer what a protein can bind or move from the geometry, chemical complementarity, and conformational transitions shown.
No hard prerequisite is declared. Treat every supplied protein diagram as a relationship map rather than as a demand to recall a full protein catalog.
Selective binding depends on three-dimensional complementarity: shape, charge distribution, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, hydrophobic surfaces, and other reversible interactions must align.
A mutation or denaturation can alter a binding surface without changing every residue. Function can fall when the decisive interface no longer complements its partner.
Antibodies recognize antigens through variable binding regions whose shape and chemistry complement an epitope. This lesson does not catalog immune-cell types or antibody classes.

Motor proteins use cycles of nucleotide-linked conformational change and track binding to produce directional movement. Focus on coupling between conformation, attachment, and step, not a detailed motor-family survey.

These functions are nonenzymatic outcomes even when a motor’s cycle uses ATP hydrolysis: the assessed outcome is selective binding, recognition, or mechanical movement rather than substrate catalysis.
Mental model: structure and chemical surface → partner recognition → reversible binding → conformational response → bounded biological outcome.

Think aloud: the ligand still approaches, but a pocket mutation replaces a negative group with a positive group. If the ligand presents a positive group at that contact, electrostatic complementarity is lost, so binding should weaken. I do not infer a whole immune pathway.

Worked example: an antibody binding site has a hydrophobic pocket and a negatively charged edge. Antigen epitope A presents a matching hydrophobic protrusion and positive edge; epitope B has the wrong shape and a negative edge. A is predicted to bind more strongly.
Selection reasoning: recognition follows the supplied interface complementarity, not the size of the entire antigen.
Guided practice: use the visible condition-to-behavior frame, then commit before feedback.
Less help: apply the same model with a brief non-answer-bearing cue.
On your own: analyze a fresh protein case without answer-bearing help.
Boundary: “fits” does not mean permanent covalent attachment. Binding is often reversible, and motor movement requires repeated attachment and release rather than one maximally tight interaction.
Near exit: apply the taught model independently in a closely aligned case.
Changed exit: preserve the construct while the representation or required inference changes.
Near-function repair: Evaluate the actual interface: aligned shape and chemistry, not unrelated whole-system details. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh near re-entry: recheck the exact function in an unexposed case.
Changed-function repair: Motor function couples track-binding cycles with conformational changes that generate steps. The fresh re-entry remains unexposed.
Fresh changed re-entry: recheck the exact failed function in a new representation.
Bounded stop: after one fresh re-entry miss, do not loop or award exit credit. Return control to the planner.
Recap: locate the decisive interface, compare shape and chemistry, predict binding or recognition, and connect conformational cycling to directional movement.
